summary: Clarifies how to handle the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData content type when more than one digital signature is present. It updates the CMS specification, RFC 3852, so implementations treat multiple signers consistently. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When several people sign the same letter, readers need clear rules about how to check every signature. This note spells out those rules.

questions: how does cms handle multiple signers
why use multiple signatures for the same content
subtitle: Clarifies how to handle multiple digital signatures in signed messages

tldr.problem: The original CMS specification did not clearly explain how to handle signed content with multiple digital signatures from the same signer.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC clarifies that receiving one valid signature from a signer counts as that signer successfully signing the content, even if other signatures from the same signer are present or fail.
tldr.outcome: Implementations now have clear rules for multiple signatures, making it easier to support algorithm negotiation and migration during hash function or algorithm transitions.

today: RFC 4853 updates RFC 3852 to provide clearer rules for handling multiple signatures. RFC 3852 itself was later obsoleted by RFC 5652, which incorporated these clarifications.

sections.title: The Multiple-Signer Problem
sections.content:
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is a standard format for signed, encrypted, and authenticated messages. The SignedData content type in CMS allows one signer to attach multiple digital signatures to the same content, but the original specification in RFC 3852 did not make clear how recipients should interpret this.

This document updates RFC 3852 to clarify that when a single signer provides multiple signatures, recipients should treat the content as validly signed by that signer if any one of those signatures is valid. The application does not need to verify all of them.
sections.eli5: Imagine you sign a letter, but you write your name with three different pens in case the reader can only see some colors. The letter is still just signed once by you, even though your name appears three times.

sections.title: Why Signers Use Multiple Signatures
sections.content:
There are two main practical reasons for a signer to create multiple signatures on the same content. First, different recipients may support different signature algorithms. For example, some recipients might only support RSA, while others only support ECDSA. A signer can generate both an RSA signature and an ECDSA signature so that each recipient can verify the one it understands.

Second, communities sometimes transition from older to newer algorithms or hash functions. During the migration from SHA-1 to SHA-256, for example, a signer can produce both a SHA-1-based signature and a SHA-256-based signature. This way, recipients that still only understand the older algorithm can verify one signature, while those that have upgraded can verify the other.
sections.eli5: Some people read only English, some only Spanish. If you want everyone to understand your letter, you might write it in both languages. Your message is still one, just available in two forms.

sections.title: What This Clarification Means
sections.content:
The updated specification makes two key points. First, when more than one signature from a given signer is present, successful validation of just one of them counts as successful signing by that signer. Second, applications that require different rules (for example, requiring all signatures to be valid) must explicitly state those rules in their own specification.

The clarification also notes that when determining whether multiple signatures come from the same signer, simple matching of the signer's identifier is usually sufficient, but some applications may need more sophisticated matching rules.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: if you see a valid signature from someone, the message is signed by that person, even if you also see other signatures from them that don't work or that you don't recognize.
